title: Better Decisions · Episode 1
chapters: Opportunity cost: the hidden price of every choice
Mental models: a toolkit for thinking

units.t: Better Decisions. Episode one.
In this episode: How to make better decisions, Opportunity cost: the hidden price of every choice, Mental models: a toolkit for thinking and Understanding risk.
Part one. How to make better decisions.
Practical tools from psychology and economics for the choices that actually matter.
Match effort to stakes.
We make thousands of decisions a day, and treating them all seriously is exhausting.
A useful filter, popularised by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, asks whether a decision is a 'one-way door' or a 'two-way door'.
One-way doors, like selling a house or quitting a career, are hard to reverse and deserve careful thought.
Two-way doors, like trying a new gym or ordering a dish, can be undone, so decide quickly and learn.
Most are two-way.
Psychologist Barry Schwartz adds two styles: maximisers hunt for the very best option, while satisficers set criteria and pick the first option that meets them.
Maximisers sometimes land better outcomes, such as higher starting salaries, but feel less satisfied and more regretful.
For most choices, define 'good enough' first, then stop when you find it.
Fewer options, true costs.
In a famous 2000 study, shoppers who saw 24 jams were more likely to stop but far less likely to buy than those who saw 6.
Later research found choice overload isn't universal; it depends on how complex the options are and how clear your preferences are.
Still, when faced with too many options, narrow them fast: pick your top two or three criteria, drop anything that fails them, and compare only the finalists.
Then count the opportunity cost, the value of the best alternative you give up.
A $60,000 car costs more than $60,000; it also costs what that money could have become, or the holiday you won't take.
An evening of scrolling costs the book not read or the friend not called.
Asking 'What else could I do with this?'
makes invisible costs visible.
Slow the feelings.
Working memory holds only a few items, so decisions juggled in our heads get dominated by whichever factor feels loudest.
Writing helps.
Charles Darwin famously listed the pros and cons of marriage before proposing.
Better still, weight each factor from 1 to 5 by how much it matters, and score how well each option performs.
You needn't follow the numbers blindly, but the process often reveals what you really care about.
Emotions in the moment can also hijack decisions, so try the 10/10/10 test suggested by writer Suzy Welch: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years?
Or take the outsider view and ask, 'What would I tell my best friend to do?'
We often reason more wisely about other people's problems.
Set tripwires.
Many decisions go wrong not at the start but months later, when we keep pushing on after the evidence has turned, partly because of the time and money already spent.
Brothers Chip and Dan Heath, in their 2013 book Decisive, suggest setting tripwires: before committing, write down the signals that would make you stop or reconsider.
'If the renovation runs 20% over budget, we pause and rethink.'
'If this job still feels wrong in six months, I start looking.'
Drawing the line while you're calm makes it far easier to act later, when pride and money already spent are urging you to keep going.
Judge the process.
Former poker champion Annie Duke warns against 'resulting': judging a decision by how it turned out.
A good decision can have a bad outcome because of luck, and a reckless one can work out fine.
If you drive home drunk and arrive safely, it was still a bad decision.
Instead, judge the process: did you have reasonable information, consider alternatives and think about risks?
Keeping a simple decision journal, noting what you decided and why, helps you learn from both luck and skill over time.
The key idea: Decide small, reversible choices quickly and aim for 'good enough', saving careful thought for one-way doors.
Part two. Opportunity cost: the hidden price of every choice.
Everything you choose to do means something else you didn't.
Economists call that missing alternative the opportunity cost, and it changes how you see every decision.
The cost you can't see.
Say you've got a free Saturday and $100, and spend both at a music festival.
The ticket price is obvious, but what else did that day cost?
Perhaps a beach trip with friends, a shift that would have paid $200, or a lazy day of rest.
Economists call the value of the best option you gave up the opportunity cost.
It matters because every choice involves a trade off, even when no money changes hands.
The festival might still be right.
The point is not guilt, but seeing clearly what you're choosing between, rather than only noticing the price tag.
No free lunch.
The saying 'there's no such thing as a free lunch' was popularised by Milton Friedman.
It dates back to American saloons that offered free food to customers who bought drinks; the cost was built into the price of beer.
The same logic applies widely.
A free app may be paid for with your data and attention.
A free park was paid for with taxes, and the land could have been used for housing.
Your own time is never free, because an hour scrolling is an hour not spent sleeping, exercising or talking to someone you love.
Recognising hidden costs doesn't mean refusing free things.
It means knowing what you're trading.
Time is scarcest.
Money can be earned again, but time only runs one way, so it's a key place to think about opportunity cost.
Should you spend two hours driving across town to save $20?
It depends on what else those hours could give you.
Studying for a qualification means giving up income or leisure now for higher earnings or more satisfying work later.
A big cost of university for many students is not the fees but the wages they could have earned instead.
None of these choices has a universal right answer.
Opportunity cost turns a vague feeling into a clearer question: is this the best use of my time?
Seen, unseen, sunk.
In 1850 Frederic Bastiat told the parable of the broken window.
A boy smashes a shop window, and onlookers say at least the glazier gets work.
Bastiat asked about the unseen: the shopkeeper would have spent that money elsewhere, perhaps on shoes, so the shoemaker loses what the glazier gains, and the town is a window poorer.
When someone says a project will create jobs, ask what the money would otherwise have done.
Sunk costs work the other way.
If you paid $150 for a concert ticket but you're sick and it's pouring, that $150 is gone whether you go or not.
The only question is whether the night out beats staying home now.
Throwing good resources after bad to avoid admitting a loss is the real waste.
Using the idea well.
Textbooks illustrate opportunity cost with 'guns and butter': with limited workers and materials, more military spending means fewer civilian goods.
Budgets work the same way.
Funding a hospital, road, tax cut or defence program means not spending that money elsewhere, or borrowing and paying interest later.
Asking 'compared with what?'
is a powerful question in politics.
Taken too far, the idea could make life miserable, as if every coffee should have been invested.
It works best for decisions that matter: a job offer, a big purchase, a windfall, or whether to keep pouring effort into something that isn't working.
Before a significant choice, name the realistic next best alternative out loud.
You'll choose with open eyes, and sometimes rest or fun is the best use of your time.
The key idea: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you gave up, even when no money changes hands.
Part three. Mental models: a toolkit for thinking.
The best thinkers don't know everything.
They carry a handful of reliable ways of seeing, and reach for the right one at the right moment.
A latticework of ideas.
A mental model is a simplified picture of how something works, like supply and demand or compound interest.
Everyone uses them, mostly without noticing.
Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's long-time partner, argued in a 1994 talk that you need a 'latticework' of models from many fields: economics, psychology, physics, biology and more.
His warning was the saying 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail'.
If you only know one way of seeing, you'll force every problem into it.
A few broadly useful models, practised until they become habits, can sharpen almost any decision.
First principles, inversion.
Mostly we reason by analogy, doing what others do.
First-principles thinking, an idea going back to Aristotle, strips a problem back to what is fundamentally true, then reasons up.
Ask what we are sure of and what is merely assumed.
If a bathroom renovation quote seems huge, list the parts: materials, labour, waterproofing, plumbing, permits.
You may find which are negotiable.
It's slower, so save it for problems that matter.
Inversion, 'invert, always invert', often credited to mathematician Carl Jacobi, flips the question.
Instead of 'how do I succeed?'
, ask 'what would make this fail?'
and avoid it.
Imagine a project failed a year from now and ask why; Gary Klein calls this a pre-mortem.
Second-order thinking.
First-order thinking stops at the immediate result: this price cut wins customers.
Second-order thinking keeps asking 'and then what?'
Competitors may cut prices too, and everyone earns less.
A widely told story, possibly exaggerated, describes a bounty on cobras in colonial Delhi that led people to breed cobras for the reward.
Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the 'cobra effect' names a real pattern: well-meant rules that create the opposite of what was intended.
Before acting, sketch the likely reactions of the people and systems affected, over months, not just days.
Margin of safety.
Engineers don't design a bridge to carry exactly the heaviest expected truck; they build it for several times that load.
Investor Benjamin Graham, Warren Buffett's teacher, borrowed the idea for finance as a 'margin of safety': buy only when the price is well below your estimate of value, in case you're wrong.
It works in everyday life too.
Leave 20 minutes spare for the airport run.
Add a contingency of 10 to 20% to a renovation budget.
Borrow less than the bank says you can.
We're reliably over-optimistic about how long things take and what they cost, so a buffer isn't pessimism; it's realism.
The less reversible the decision, the bigger the margin you want.
Know your limits.
Buffett and Munger describe a 'circle of competence': areas where you truly understand how things work.
Outside it, confidence is dangerous, because you don't know what you don't know.
What matters is knowing where its edge is.
Outside it, slow down, seek real expertise and prefer small, reversible bets.
'The map is not the territory', a phrase from Alfred Korzybski in the early 1930s, reminds us that budgets, forecasts and dashboards leave things out.
When map and ground disagree, trust the ground.
Related is Chesterton's fence: before removing a rule that seems pointless, find out why it was put there.
Use models as questions: what's true here, what would guarantee failure, and then what?
Practise on small decisions, and use several.
The key idea: A mental model is a simplified picture of how something works, and having several beats relying on one.
Part four. Understanding risk.
People fear sharks and plane crashes, then drive home tired without a second thought.
Our risk radar is badly calibrated, and it can be fixed.
Why we misjudge risk.
Humans didn't evolve to read statistics.
We judge danger with fast, emotional shortcuts.
Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic: we rate something as more likely when examples spring easily to mind.
Shark attacks and plane crashes get saturation news coverage, so they feel common.
Heart disease, falls at home and car crashes rarely make headlines, so they feel ordinary.
Paul Slovic and other researchers found we also fear risks that feel uncontrollable, unfamiliar or imposed on us far more than risks we choose.
Australia records a handful of fatal shark bites a year, yet around 300 or more people drown, many in rivers, lakes and backyard pools.
Dread risks.
A 'dread risk' is a rare event that kills many people at once, such as a plane crash or terrorist attack.
It triggers fear far beyond its statistical danger.
After the September 11 attacks in 2001, many Americans avoided flying and drove instead.
Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer estimated the extra driving caused roughly 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year, more than the passengers killed on the four hijacked planes.
Australia's road toll runs at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 deaths a year, plus tens of thousands of serious injuries.
Qantas has never had a fatal jet accident, and per kilometre, flying on a major airline is many times safer than driving.
The riskiest part of a trip is often the drive to the airport.
Relative versus absolute.
Headlines love relative risk: 'X doubles your risk of Y'.
But doubling a tiny risk still leaves a tiny risk.
In 1995, UK authorities warned that newer contraceptive pills doubled the risk of a type of blood clot.
The absolute increase was roughly from 1 in 7,000 women to 2 in 7,000.
Many women stopped taking the pill, and researchers later linked the scare to a rise in unplanned pregnancies and abortions, which carry their own risks.
Whenever you hear 'increases risk by 50%', ask: 50% of what?
How many people out of 1,000 or 10,000 are actually affected?
Ignoring base rates.
The base rate is how often something happens in the first place, and we routinely ignore it when a good story comes along.
Kahneman and Tversky described 'Steve': shy, tidy and helpful, with a passion for detail.
Is he more likely a librarian or a farmer?
Most people say librarian, because he fits the stereotype.
But in the United States there were more than 20 male farmers for every male librarian, so Steve is far more likely to farm.
The same trap catches us with a 'sure thing' share tip, a start-up that looks like the next big success, or a stranger who 'looks suspicious'.
Before judging by fit, ask how common it is.
Deciding better.
Good risk thinking asks four questions.
How likely is it, in absolute terms?
How bad would it be, and is it reversible?
Compared with what, including the risk of the alternative?
Can I cheaply reduce it?
Say '3 in 1,000' rather than '0.
3%', and notice when a vivid story is doing the work data should.
The biggest killers are slow and familiar: heart disease, dementia, cancers, smoking and inactivity, plus falls among older Australians.
Put effort into seatbelts, not driving tired, pool fences, sun protection and health checks.
Zero risk doesn't exist; doing nothing carries risk too.
Researchers compare activities in 'micromorts', a one-in-a-million chance of death.
For medical choices, ask your doctor to explain the numbers in plain terms.
The key idea: We judge risk by how vivid and emotional it feels, not by how likely it is.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What should you do with a 'two-way door' decision?
Answer. Decide quickly, since it can be undone.
Question two. What is the opportunity cost of attending the festival in this example?
Answer. The value of the best alternative, such as a paid shift.
Question three. What risk does 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail' describe?
Answer. Forcing every problem into one familiar approach.
Question four. What does the availability heuristic lead us to do?
Answer. Judge a risk as likelier when examples come easily.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
